note: V90Jd.cpp is the constructor, the destructor and the two packing leaves.  The constructor is where this set is aimed: it is fourteen stores and two loops, and the whole of what it can get wrong is WHICH bit of the parameter reaches WHICH byte of the message.  So most of the mutations below transpose a pair or move a loop bound by one -- the failures a comparison of the two objects can see and a reading of the disassembly can miss.  Two entries cover the CRC in getBitVector so the file's older half is not left unmeasured now that it has a suite.

label: the two lookahead bits are transposed
the two constellation parameters are transposed
the constellation bits carry the whole word, not its low byte
the first rate group is one bit short
find:
for (i = 0; i <= 15; i++)
		bits[V90JD_GROUP1 + 1 + i] = (unsigned char)((mask >> i) & 1);
replace:
for (i = 0; i <= 14; i++)
		bits[V90JD_GROUP1 + 1 + i] = (unsigned char)((mask >> i) & 1);

label: the second rate group stops where V92Jd's does
the second rate group starts one bit low in the mask
the rate mask is read from the wrong parameter
the unpacker's word is left as it was
the unpacker's second byte is left as it was
the CRC's two feedback taps are transposed
the destructor is not empty
why: GCC's `-flifetime-dse` is on at -O2 and deletes stores to `*this` in a destructor, so the mutated body and the empty one compile to the identical bare `ret`.  The same entry appears in v90params.json and v92params.json for the same reason: no mutation confined to the destroyed object can be caught here, which is also the reason the test asserts the destructor wrote nothing rather than relying on a mutation to say so.
